title: Circle and Proof Demo Verified-ID Stablecoin Payments for AI Agents
snippet: The two firms are combining Proof's x401 identity protocol with Circle's USDC Agent Wallets to let merchants trust and settle AI agent purchases. The post Circle and Proof Demo Verified-ID Stablecoin Payments for AI Agents appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Circle Internet Group (NYSE: CRCL) and identity infrastructure firm Proof have unveiled a collaboration at Money20/20 in Las Vegas last week, demonstrating how verified legal identity and stablecoin payments can be combined in a single agent-initiated transaction. The demo addresses one of the more pressing structural problems in agentic commerce: merchants currently have no reliable way to know who authorised a purchase made by an AI agent, leaving them to choose between blocking agents outright or accepting the associated fraud and chargeback risk.

How the protocols fit together

Pat Kinsel, founder and chief executive of Proof

The integration draws on two open HTTP-layer standards. Proof’s x401 protocol, published in June 2026 and moved into production last week, uses the HTTP 401 “Unauthorised” response to let a merchant specify what identity proof it requires and which credential issuers it trusts. Circle’s x402 protocol uses the HTTP 402 “Payment Required” response to specify how the agent should pay. Used in sequence, x401 answers who the agent acts for, and x402 answers how it settles the transaction.

In the demo flow, a merchant responds to an inbound agent request with both an x401 identity requirement and an x402 USDC payment request. The agent’s Proof wallet presents a verified credential derived from identity proofing certified to NIST IAL2 standard, accompanied by a signed, purchase-specific approval. Only the relevant identity facts are disclosed; no full ID document is transmitted or stored by the merchant. The agent then pays from a Circle Agent Wallet in USDC over x402. The merchant retains signed, tamper-evident evidence of who authorised the transaction, which can be used in dispute resolution without requiring Proof to be called again in real time.

A secondary mechanism embedded in the protocol stack is commercially notable. Proof prices identity claims individually, and the same x402 channel can route a micropayment from the merchant to the identity issuer for each verification used. That removes the bilateral contract requirement that has historically limited the reuse of verified identity across ecosystems: a merchant can pay for a check on the spot, at the moment it needs it, without a prior sales relationship with the credential issuer.

Pat Kinsel, founder and chief executive of Proof, said: “Our demo with Circle shows one exchange can answer both questions: verified identity from Proof and payment in USDC. That gives businesses a reason to say yes to agents instead of blocking them.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The timing is pointed. Several large institutions at Money20/20 are understood to be blocking AI agent traffic entirely, a posture that carries its own commercial cost as consumer adoption of AI assistants accelerates. The Proof and Circle approach is one of several competing frameworks attempting to resolve agentic identity, alongside emerging work in the W3C verifiable credentials ecosystem and proprietary agent-authentication layers from payment networks and cloud providers.

From a regulatory perspective, the NIST IAL2 credential anchor is significant. That standard is referenced in US federal identity frameworks and is gaining traction in Know Your Customer discussions as a benchmark for remote identity proofing. In the UK, the Digital Identity and Attributes Trust Framework published by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology sets comparable requirements, suggesting that a credential meeting IAL2 could attract recognition in cross-border contexts. The European eIDAS 2.0 wallet framework similarly defines trust levels against which x401-type presentations could eventually be assessed. Whether regulators will accept protocol-layer identity assertions as satisfying KYC obligations under anti-money laundering rules remains an open question, and one that will shape how quickly financial institutions can adopt agent-native payment flows rather than routing them through existing customer-authenticated channels.

title: Henry Dannell Opens DIFC Office to Serve Cross-Border HNW Clients
snippet: The UK specialist credit adviser has established a representative office in Dubai to serve internationally mobile high-net-worth individuals and family offices. The post Henry Dannell Opens DIFC Office to Serve Cross-Border HNW Clients appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Henry Dannell, a UK-based specialist cross-border credit adviser, has opened a representative office in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), marking the firm’s first foothold in the Middle East. The office, which operates as a representative of Henry Dannell Private Clients Limited, an FCA-authorised entity, is intended to serve internationally mobile entrepreneurs, family offices and high-net-worth individuals whose borrowing requirements span multiple jurisdictions.

Founded in 2019, the firm positions itself as a specialist structurer of bespoke credit solutions rather than a conventional mortgage provider. Its advisory team, which it says holds over 165 years of combined industry experience, works across residential, commercial and specialist lending for clients with unconventional income profiles or internationally distributed assets.

Why Dubai, why now

Kem Kemal, co-founder and CEO at Henry Dannell

The choice of DIFC is unsurprising given the centre’s regulatory architecture and the calibre of its tenant base. DIFC operates under its own legal and regulatory framework, overseen by the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), and functions as a gateway for institutions seeking regional access with internationally recognised governance standards. For a firm regulated by the FCA and working with clients across multiple jurisdictions, DIFC’s structural familiarity reduces friction in both compliance and client engagement.

Dubai’s appeal as a wealth management hub has grown materially over the past several years, driven by inflows of capital from Europe, South Asia and Russia following geopolitical disruption. Family offices and ultra-high-net-worth individuals have relocated in significant numbers, and the demand for sophisticated, multi-jurisdictional financial advice has risen correspondingly. That demand has not gone unnoticed by advisers and lenders, with a growing number of UK and European wealth firms establishing Gulf presences.

Chief executive and co-founder Kem Kemal said the firm exists precisely because conventional lenders have been slow to adapt to the realities of modern international wealth. “Too often, highly accomplished individuals with substantial assets and strong financial positions encounter challenges because their circumstances fall outside conventional frameworks,” he said. “Our role is to understand the complete picture and design bespoke solutions that reflect the realities of modern international wealth.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The cross-border lending advisory segment is not without regulatory complexity. Henry Dannell’s DIFC presence is structured as a representative office rather than a fully licensed DFSA-regulated entity, which limits the range of regulated activities it can undertake directly in the region. Relationship-building and referral activity are permissible; executing regulated financial services for UAE-resident clients would require separate DFSA authorisation. The firm has acknowledged this by describing the Dubai operation explicitly as a first phase, suggesting a licence application may follow if commercial traction justifies it.

More broadly, the segment sits at an intersection that regulators across multiple jurisdictions are scrutinising more closely. The OECD’s Common Reporting Standard and the UK’s increasing focus on offshore asset disclosure mean that clients structuring borrowing against internationally held assets must navigate a more complex compliance environment than a decade ago. Advisers who can demonstrate command of that environment have a genuine differentiator; those who cannot face material liability risk.

Henry Dannell’s next disclosures to watch will be whether it progresses to full DFSA authorisation, which regional professional advisory partners it formalises, and whether it publishes transaction volumes or client numbers that substantiate the commercial rationale for the office.

title: UK-Nigeria Remittance Rivals Battle on Rates and Banking Features
snippet: New analysis of the £2.8bn UK-Nigeria corridor finds Africhange, LemFi and NALA competing on FX rates, scale and embedded banking. The post UK-Nigeria Remittance Rivals Battle on Rates and Banking Features appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Africhange, LemFi and NALA are intensifying their rivalry along the UK-Nigeria remittance corridor as competition shifts beyond foreign exchange rates toward embedded banking services, savings products and deposit protection, according to a new market analysis published in October 2026.

The corridor processes an estimated £2.8 billion annually, making it the largest cross-border payments channel between the UK and Africa and the third largest from the UK to any single country, according to data cited from the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford.

The pricing battleground

Exchange rates remain the sharpest point of differentiation. An analysis of more than 37,000 matched price comparisons, drawn from aggregator platform BestRates and covering January 2025 to August 2026, found that Africhange delivered higher GBP-to-NGN payout quotes than LemFi in over 90% of instances, averaging an additional NGN 12.69 per pound sterling.

The analysis cautions, however, that static historical comparisons capture only part of the picture, given that live FX rates shift throughout the trading day. Fee structures also vary: Africhange and LemFi both operate zero-transfer-fee models, while NALA uses a hybrid approach, charging a flat £0.99 fee on direct bank payouts and waiving fees on mobile-money channels.

LemFi’s competitive response rests on institutional scale rather than spot-rate aggression. Backed by a $53 million Series B completed in early 2025, the company reported crossing two million global users and processing approximately $1 billion in monthly transaction volume. NALA, meanwhile, serves more than one million users across 35 countries, with a pan-African coverage model targeting both consumer remittances and cross-border business payments.

The super-app pivot

All three operators are pursuing product expansion that goes well beyond the transfer itself. Africhange has partnered with UK-licensed bank Griffin to offer customers dedicated GBP current accounts with individual sort codes and account numbers. The arrangement brings Financial Services Compensation Scheme deposit protection of up to £85,000, a regulatory feature that is uncommon among pure-play remittance providers and one that materially raises the trust threshold for customers considering holding balances rather than simply sending them.

LemFi has added yield-bearing savings products and credit-monitoring tools to its app. NALA is rolling out its Global Account suite, which targets freelancers and small businesses with multi-currency holding and conversion across US dollars, sterling and local African currencies.

David Ajala, chief executive of Africhange, said: “The UK-Nigeria payment highway is undergoing a fundamental transformation from a basic remittance corridor into an embedded banking battleground. The challenge is finding the right balance between price, reliability, scale and a broader range of financial services that gives customers a reason to stay.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The strategic direction described here reflects a wider pattern across the African diaspora payments segment. Several well-capitalised operators, including WorldRemit and Wise, are also present on high-volume African corridors, and the competitive pressure from aggregator transparency tools has compressed FX margins industry-wide.

From a regulatory standpoint, UK payment institutions serving diaspora senders operate under FCA oversight, and the Consumer Duty rules that came into force in 2023 place explicit obligations on firms to demonstrate fair value in their pricing. The FSCS partnership that Africhange has structured through Griffin is a notable differentiator in this context, as it effectively converts a remittance app into a deposit-taking relationship in the eyes of the customer, with the protection that implies. Rivals pursuing savings features without a banking licence or a licensed partner face a narrower product envelope under current FCA authorisation frameworks.

The analysis suggests that, for the corridor’s next phase, competitive advantage will rest less on who posts the sharpest daily rate and more on who captures the broader financial relationship of the UK-based Nigerian diaspora.

title: Budget 2026: founders backed, banks taxed, and a fintech catch
snippet: Healey's first Budget backs founders and taxes banks harder for 15 months. Fintech specialists welcome most of it, but warn the new relief may miss fintechs. The post Budget 2026: founders backed, banks taxed, and a fintech catch appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
John Healey‘s first Budget gave founders a 10 per cent capital gains rate and doubled a key share option limit, and asked banks to pay twice the corporation tax surcharge for 15 months.

The fintech and finance specialists who sent reaction to The Fintech Times welcomed most of the founder package. The sharpest warning came from fintech’s own trade body: as drafted, the new relief may not reach fintechs at all.

The founder package

The centrepiece for start-ups is a new Founders’ Relief. From 6 April 2027, qualifying founders of high-growth, innovative companies will pay capital gains tax at 10 per cent on up to £10 million of lifetime gains. Who qualifies is still being settled: the detailed design is out for technical consultation, and the measure will be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27.

For a narrow group, it reverses a long retreat. Entrepreneurs’ Relief, renamed Business Asset Disposal Relief, had its lifetime limit cut from £10 million to £1 million in 2020, and its rate has since risen from 10 per cent to 18 per cent. The same Budget halves that limit again, to £500,000 from April 2027, so most people selling a business get less relief while a smaller set of high-growth founders get more. On share options, the Company Share Option Plan is relaunched as EMI2, and from 6 April 2027 employees will be able to hold tax-advantaged options worth up to £120,000, double the current £60,000, with the overlap with the Enterprise Management Incentive limit removed.

Arjun Kumar, co-founder of tax software firm Taxd, summed up the reception among founders: “This is a Budget with the right ambition for people who build things: founders’ relief back on the table, better share options, support for young entrepreneurs and a real plan to give cities their own money. But it asks the self-employed to pay tax more often and hits landlords for the third time in two years. Builders are being backed; earners and landlords are paying.”

Janine Hirt, chief executive of Innovate Finance, the industry body for UK fintech, welcomed the share option changes, noting that “many UK FinTechs rely on employee share options to attract and retain staff, making equity a core part of remuneration for ordinary workers.” The relief itself is another matter. “Proposals for a new Founders Relief appear at first glance to reverse the reductions in business asset disposal relief which were made in 2020, for a smaller group of high growth entrepreneurs,” she said. “This is welcome in principle but the eligibility must be extended beyond today’s proposals, which would currently exclude financial services and therefore most FinTechs.”

She added that “some FinTechs remain excluded from the Enterprise Management Incentive scheme and we would encourage this to be reviewed.” Hirt set out Innovate Finance’s wider case in her column for The Fintech Times on the morning of the Budget.

Andy Oury, tax partner at accountancy firm Oury Clark, questioned whether a relief built around founders fits how companies actually grow. “In my experience it’s often not Founders who end up progressing a business to its full potential. Others join along the way as managers, owners and investors,” he said. “It’s a shame Healey didn’t simply revive Entrepreneurs Relief to recognise and incentivise the different parties in the architecture of the SME system that contribute to business growth. But let’s see what the fine print says.”

Non-competes: promised, not yet

The Budget confirms the government will legislate so that non-compete clauses no longer stop start-ups and scaling firms from hiring. It will consult first on the wider use of restrictive practices and set out a detailed position in early 2027, ahead of legislation. Jonno Evans, partner at venture capital firm IQ Capital, said reform “will make it easier for talented individuals to move between companies, launch new ventures and turn innovative ideas into successful businesses.” Emmanuelle Ries, employment partner at Kingsley Napley, read the timetable differently: “The promise to launch a further consultation in early 2027 before legislating pushes this into the medium to long grass. Clearly change is not imminent.”

Banks pay more, for now

The corporation tax surcharge on banks rises from 3 per cent to 6 per cent from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028, to help pay for the £100 Household Energy Payment. The Budget says the 15-month period will be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27 and will not be extended. The surcharge was introduced at 8 per cent in 2016 and cut to 3 per cent in April 2023, when the profits threshold below which banks pay nothing was raised to £100 million.

David Postings, chief executive of UK Finance, said: “Increasing bank taxes is not, in our view, the best way to deliver growth. The Chancellor’s promise that this increase will be time-limited is therefore important, given we already have a tax regime that needs to be made more internationally competitive.”

For challenger banks the threshold matters more than the rate. Hirt pointed out that the surcharge “maintains its £100 million threshold which has historically exempted new banks,” but argued that “in the long term the threshold needs to be raised to provide headroom for our growing digital banks who have been passing interest rates on to savers and are now providing the majority of lending to small firms across the UK.” She also welcomed the Chancellor’s remit letter to the Bank of England‘s Financial Policy Committee, which asks for the next stage of its review of bank capital requirements to make the framework more internationally competitive and to promote competition.

Anil Oncu, CEO of payments firm Bitpace, expects the cost to travel down the chain. “When tier-one clearing banks absorb higher corporate surcharges, mid-market merchants and exporters feel it through higher FX margins, SWIFT fees and account facility charges,” he said.

Capital for small firms

The Budget lifts the British Business Bank‘s financial capacity by £5 billion to £30.6 billion, including £1.4 billion more for equity funds backing high-growth businesses and £450 million for a new venture debt product.

Kristaps Zips, UK CEO of payabl., called it “a welcome announcement from the Chancellor” for fintechs looking to scale, adding: “Fintech has long been one of the UK’s biggest success stories and the key now is making sure this support reaches the businesses that need it.”

Lenders closer to the high street were less impressed. Rob Keown-Boyd, CEO of non-bank SME lender multifi, said the measures “simply don’t go far enough to help the SMEs that are facing a cashflow crisis,” and pointed to his own book: “demand for working capital has kept climbing through 2026; applications are running around a third higher than the same point last year.”

Paul Joyce, partner at mid-market M&A adviser LAVA Advisory Partners, raised a practical question: “You can put a considerable sum behind a scheme and still leave someone running a perfectly good business scratching their head about whether any of it is available to them.”

For open finance, Hirt welcomed a commitment she said Innovate Finance had asked for: the government will explore the use of HMRC data in Open Finance, working with regulators and industry to test feasibility, which she sees as a way to unlock finance for small firms and the self-employed.

Paying tax sooner

From April 2029, people who already make Payments on Account for Income Tax Self Assessment will make smaller, more regular payments through the year instead of two large instalments. Kumar called it “the single biggest revenue raiser in the Budget,” adding: “it comes from cashflow, not from a rate. Cashflow is what kills small businesses.” Oury expects the change in collection to bite hard in its first year: “the transition will be brutal. It will mean roughly eighteen months of tax squeezed into twelve. This could be a solvency event for some.”

E-invoicing gets a date

The Budget confirmed that VAT invoices must be issued in a specified electronic format from 1 April 2029, published an implementation roadmap, and committed to full details of the policy and technical design by April 2028. Pierre Arman, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal, warned that “the full details of the UK e-invoicing regime may not be known until April 2028, which would leave businesses with little time to get ready and could threaten business continuity.”

Alex Baulf, VP of global indirect tax at Avalara, took the opposite view of the same roadmap: “After years of watching Europe press ahead, UK businesses can now stop guessing about e-invoicing. This roadmap provides the clarity organisations have been waiting for and turns April 2029 into a date they can actively prepare for.”

Abigail Myers-Antiaye, VP of global compliance at Basware, pointed to France, where a mandate is already rolling out: “choosing an approved provider did not fix inaccurate customer records or bills that did not match what had been ordered.” Her advice was to start internal preparation now: “Leaving existing invoicing problems untouched means paying to carry them into a new system.”

Markets shrug, for now

Joe Calnan, head of FX dealing at iBanFirst, gave the Budget “15 out of 20. Not because it offers convincing solutions to the UK’s structural economic challenges, but because the exercise was exceptionally difficult, even more so under a new Prime Minister.” He does not expect it to change monetary policy, and still expects the Bank of England to raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points next week.

Todd Laddusaw, CFO at treasury platform Kyriba, cautioned against reading too much into the calm: “The biggest mistake businesses can make after today’s Budget is to mistake a relatively calm market reaction for a clean bill of financial health.” With the next rate decision on 5 November, he said, “the cost of capital remains a moving target.”

What comes next

The Bank of England announces its next interest rate decision on 5 November. The higher bank surcharge applies from 1 January 2027, and the government’s detailed position on non-competes is due in early 2027. Founders’ Relief, EMI2 and the lower £500,000 limit for Business Asset Disposal Relief all take effect from April 2027. Full e-invoicing details are due by April 2028, ahead of the April 2029 mandate.

Source: HM Treasury, Budget 2026

title: Settling cross-border payments remains tough
snippet: Global payments are moving faster, but local settlement remains a pain point for many companies, according to speakers on a Money20/20 panel.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Global payments are moving faster, but local settlement remains a pain point for many companies, according to speakers on a Money20/20 panel.

        

            

        Published Oct. 29, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                An exhibition hall sign greeted attendees at the 2026 Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.
            
        
            Justin Bachman/Payments Dive
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Settlement of a cross-border payment at its destination remains a pain point across the industry, despite improvements in rails, speed and interoperability among players, payments executives said last week in a panel discussion.

The last portion of a cross-border payment accounts for 80% of the total speed of a transaction, regardless of the payment rail or instrument that is used, said Leigh Amaro, Americas CEO for Swift, the digital financial messaging firm for international payments. Amaro spoke about how cross-border payments are evolving on Oct. 20 at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.

Given current regulations, “an instrument can leave one country looking like one thing and completely end up in another's jurisdiction looking completely different,” Debopama Sen, Citigroup’s head of payments and services, said during the discussion. “And then when you marry that with regulatory cross-border restriction challenges, the last mile is where our clients struggle, and the last mile does need to be addressed.”

Dive Insight:

Cross-border payments totaled about $190 trillion last year, generating about $290 billion in revenue for the payments industry, according to an August report from the consulting firm McKinsey.

Three-quarters of Swift-enabled payments reach the recipient’s beneficiary bank within 10 minutes, Amaro said. At that point, however, local rules, operating hours and other challenges slow the settlement process, regardless of whether a payment was sent via stablecoin, tokenized deposit or a traditional rail, she said.

Meanwhile, regulators in many countries are pushing for more price transparency with respect to the services, while compliance complexity has increased due to newer fintech entrants into the cross-border arena, the McKinsey report noted.

Some of the costs and complexities of cross-border payments are slowly decreasing, threatening to commoditize the field, said Jonathan Zell, a McKinsey partner in the consulting firm’s payments practice, who moderated the session.

Kush Saxena, CEO of Banking Circle Group, a Luxembourg-based fintech that specializes in cross-border payments, challenged that contention, drawing a distinction between cash and data transfers.

“I wouldn’t say moving money is a commodity. I think moving data is becoming easier,” Saxena said, noting “a ton of interoperability” the industry has created above the fiat level. “When it comes to fiat, you get into sort of regulated territory, and … there is a 180-degree divide between where global commerce is going and between where regulators are going.”

One area that Citi and other banks are working to solve is “bridging the world of blockchain and digital assets with the fiat world” in cross-border payments, Sen said. She said Citi clients have been seeking this capability “because they’re not really looking at it, saying, ‘Hey, I want to use that technology.’ They’re saying, ‘Can you solve my problem?’”

Last month, Citibank introduced a cross-border, instant-payment service, using its global network and collaborating with Swift, to help customers avoid the need for local banking relationships.

“Data can move at the speed of light, but that’s not enough. The cash has to be available,” Sen said, noting the success of the M-Pesa money-transfer service in Africa due to its abundant cash-payout locations in each country.

title: Finery Markets: 100 days of MiCA and the Execution Gap Banks Must Close
snippet: Finery Markets says 89% of banks now budget for digital assets, yet trading infrastructure remains the missing piece a year on. The post Finery Markets: 100 days of MiCA and the Execution Gap Banks Must Close appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
One hundred days after MiCA’s 1 July registration deadline, the headline number, 280 firms on ESMA‘s initial list, down from 2,747 operating under national transitional regimes in 2024, turns out to be the less consequential data point. According to two reports published by institutional crypto trading infrastructure firm Finery Markets in October 2026, the structural shift playing out underneath the compliance story is about liquidity, not headcount.

EURC, the euro-denominated stablecoin issued by Circle, saw volume on the Finery Markets platform rise 46 times year on year in the first nine months of 2026. Yet it still accounts for just 0.12% of total stablecoin flow through the network. Euro stablecoin supply has grown 22.6% this year to approximately $848 million, while dollar-denominated supply has been flat. The figures confirm MiCA opened a race to build native euro liquidity that remains, as the report puts it, a test of volume rather than availability.

The OTC data behind the first report covers 16 million institutional spot trades across nine months. OTC volume grew 57% year on year while the top 20 centralised exchanges collectively lost 47% of comparable activity. Stablecoins now account for 83% of trades on the network. Contributors include Banking Circle, Fipto, The Vault and identity and compliance firm Sumsub.

The execution layer banks have not built

The second report, focused on bank strategy, finds that 89% of banks have an active budget for digital assets, but only 16% have anything in production. Of the largest institutions surveyed, JPMorgan, Citi, BNY, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Standard Chartered, Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, BBVA and Revolut, nearly every live product runs on third-party rails. Custody, tokenised deposits and exchange-traded product access have been delivered. Trading has not.

That gap is the commercial proposition underlying the Finery Markets release. The firm argues that custody addresses a security question, not a revenue one. The client request that follows custody is the ability to trade held assets without routing them to an exchange the bank does not control. Building that internally requires separate bilateral liquidity relationships, each carrying its own credit agreement, fragmented pricing that complicates best-execution obligations, and a settlement infrastructure build measured in quarters rather than weeks.

Finery Markets’ alternative is a non-custodial connection to firm liquidity across more than 200 crypto and fiat pairs, with automated netting, role-based access controls and a full audit trail. Two deployment models are offered: a white-label master account in which the bank remains the regulated counterparty, and a full white-label network in which clients trade with one another and the bank typically avoids the capital requirements of a broker-dealer licence.

Regulatory context and platform updates

The regulatory read-across is substantial. In the US, the OCC has granted 16 digital asset trust charters in ten months. The GENIUS Act, MiCA, the UK’s evolving digital assets regime and Basel III capital treatment of crypto exposures are all shaping what banks can offer and at what cost. Roughly one fifth of the current MiCA register is now composed of banks, which reflects an appetite but also a compliance overhead that smaller specialist CASPs have been faster to absorb.

Finery Markets also disclosed two platform updates this month. The connectivity hub now allows institutional participants to store exchange API credentials directly within the platform interface, integrating price discovery from venues covering what the firm describes as more than two thirds of global crypto liquidity. The white-label stack has been updated with embedded API documentation, which the company says has reduced client integration timelines by a factor of 18.7 compared with a prior baseline, a figure it attributes to an AI-assisted integration repository. The 18.7 multiplier is not independently benchmarked in the release.

The firm also co-hosted a private luncheon at TOKEN2049 Singapore with Caladan, Utila and Stablecoin Insider, drawing approximately 150 professionals from OTC trading, market making, payments and stablecoin infrastructure. The consensus from those conversations, as reported by Finery Markets, was that firms growing fastest are treating routing, settlement and prefunding as infrastructure decisions rather than operational workarounds.

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering.

  

            						

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'

In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.

Notes to editors

The FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: In Profile: Kevin Lehtiniitty, CEO at Borderless.xyz
snippet: Borderless.xyz chief executive Kevin Lehtiniitty on linking stablecoins to local payment rails, the gap between announcements and reality, and compliance. The post In Profile: Kevin Lehtiniitty, CEO at Borderless.xyz appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Kevin Lehtiniitty has worked on stablecoins since before most banks had a view on them. He helped launch TrueUSD, was chief product officer at Prime Trust and later technical co-founder of Fortress, before founding Borderless.xyz.

Kevin Lehtiniitty, CEO at Borderless.xyz

Borderless.xyz gives payment companies a single API to licensed local providers, handling the conversion between stablecoins and local currency and the last-mile transfer on domestic payment rails. The company says its network now reaches 113 countries.

In this In Profile, Kevin Lehtiniitty, CEO and founder at Borderless.xyz, discusses the last mile of stablecoin payments, the gap between what is announced and what works, and why compliance needs to travel with the payment.

Tell us more about your company and its purpose

Borderless.xyz is the platform companies use to scale stablecoin payouts and collections across 113 countries on local rails.

You integrate once and get one API to the local providers in every region, 19 licensed providers across 72 currencies and 132 local rails. Each transaction covers the conversion between stablecoin and local currency and the last-mile transfer on the domestic rail, and it works with the wallet and compliance infrastructure you already have.

The platform has three main layers. Connectivity moves the money. Above it sits the operations tooling you would otherwise build, from rail monitoring to RFI case management and automated reconciliation, so adding a provider adds coverage rather than headcount. The top layer is intelligence from the network’s volume. Because we see every corridor across every provider, you can tell whether the rate you pay is competitive, and act when it isn’t.

Our purpose is to make stablecoins and local banking interoperable everywhere. Stablecoins settle in seconds but the hard part is getting it to land in local currency in your country, especially in emerging markets.

What are some of your recent achievements you’d like to highlight?

The one I’d point to first is the pilot we announced with Mastercard in August. Mastercard Crypto Credential brings a common standard and real governance to how institutions trust each other on digital asset payments. Today a receiving institution re-runs KYC on a customer the sending institution already cleared, because it has no way to rely on someone else’s compliance work. The money arrives in seconds and then waits on trust. The pilot runs that standard across our network so trust can travel with the payment.

The second is the network itself. We built the first payments network for stablecoins, and two years on it’s still the broadest, with 19 licensed providers reaching 113 countries and 72 currencies over 132 local rails. Most of that growth came from customers asking us for the next market. Every provider we add is a local expert with its own licences, so coverage grows without our customers taking on another integration.

Lastly, it’s what our customers have built on top of us. Some of the largest institutions moving stablecoins today run part of their payout and collection infrastructure on our network, and they keep adding markets on it. That’s the value of Borderless.xyz in a sentence. You go live once, and every market after that is a configuration change rather than another build.

How did you get into the fintech industry?

I’ve been working on stablecoins for more than a decade. I helped launch TrueUSD, the first fully reserved US dollar stablecoin, before USDC existed. The framework we built there held full reserves in cash and equivalents at a qualified custodian rather than on a corporate balance sheet, and had them audited. That’s recognisably what the GENIUS Act now asks of every US issuer.

Payments is really what interests me as well. It was watching what happened the moment a dollar that lived on chain needed to become a dollar in a bank account. Every hard problem sat on that boundary of fragmentation, from the banking relationships and compliance to who carries the liability when something goes wrong.

I’ve always believed the value of stablecoins is in cross-border and global transfers and spent the following years building the rails that connect the two sides, first for exchanges in the US and now for payments companies everywhere.

What’s the best thing about working in the fintech industry?

I spent more than 200 days travelling last year, because payments are local and you have to go and see that for yourself. A lot of this industry is about in-person relationships. For example, in June I was in Mexico City with our Latin American providers, and most of what we talked about was how a payout actually lands and why one into Colombia behaves so differently from one into Brazil. The people who run the rails know it, so you go meet and see it in real life.

What I keep coming back to is how much has changed in a few years. When I started in payments, a domestic transfer in most of the world meant waiting a day or two. Now you land in São Paulo and everyone from the taxi driver to the bank is on PIX, and the money moves in seconds. Same story with UPI in India and SPEI in Mexico, and dozens of other countries have built something similar. The strange part is that the moment money has to cross a border, all of that speed disappears. It goes back through correspondent banks and takes days, because the wires between countries were built for a different era. Stablecoins are the first thing that moves between countries and we’re working on the layer where those two things meet, at the moment both of them are maturing.

What frustrates you most about the fintech industry?

The gap between what is announced and what is actually working in practice can be frustrating. Every week someone announces that stablecoins have solved cross-border payments. Then you assume they’re a few weeks from launching in ten countries.

Then you actually start integrating or working with them and see the gaps. The rails listed are only supported in beta, no licence applications, broken sandboxes, etc. Announcements run well ahead of what’s live, and you can’t see any of that from the outside. A lot of what looks reliable from the outside barely works once you put real volume through it, and you only find that out after you’ve signed and started building.

That costs companies months of engineering time and a lot of credibility with their own customers. The ones that will matter in five years are the ones putting the same effort into making things work as they put into announcing them.

How have your previous roles influenced your career?

Every role handed me a different piece of the problem. At TrueUSD I worked on issuance, and the lesson there was that a stablecoin is only as good as the trust behind the reserve.

At Prime Trust I was Chief Product Officer and built the US fiat rails for exchanges like Binance US and Kraken. That’s where I quickly figured out the rails are the hard part.

Later I was the technical co-founder of Fortress and in between I spent time as the customer, one step removed from whoever owned the rails. Every compliance escalation and every stuck payment went through a middleman. I remember exactly how that felt, and Borderless is built so our customers never sit in that seat. They contract directly with the providers moving their money and own those relationships. We build the connectivity, transparency and back office tooling to scale.

What’s the best mistake you’ve ever made?

The best mistake was not shipping fast enough early on. We spent too long trying to get things right before anyone could use them, and every one of those months was a month without customer feedback. What I learned is that you don’t find out what’s wrong with a product by thinking harder about it. You find out by putting it in front of the people who have to run their business on it, and then fixing what they hit. A lot of the good decisions we’ve made came out of a customer telling us something wasn’t working, and the sooner they could tell us, the faster we could fix this moving forward.

What has the future got in store for your company?

There’s a lot in store. Several institutions are testing their onramps and offramps on our infrastructure right now, with plans to scale, and that’s why the next twelve months are the most exciting stretch we’ve had. The pieces we spent two and a half years building are starting to compound.

The network keeps growing wherever our customers pull us. Latin America and Africa are our deepest coverage today, and [Asia and the GCC] is the build for the rest of this year. We built the back office tooling to scale. The work that starts the day an integration ships is what stops most companies from ever running a second provider so continuing to build tools that allow our customers to scale seamlessly such as reconciliation, RFI case management, provider status monitoring, etc.

We’ll take what we learn from the Mastercard Crypto Credential pilot into the wider network, so compliance work done once can be trusted everywhere the payment goes.

The Benchmark is the one I’m most excited about. Every quarter it gets closer to being the public reference for what it costs to deliver a stablecoin payment into any country. I want that number to be something anyone can look up before they sign a contract. There’s more on the way that I can’t talk about yet but lots of exciting things in store.

What are the next key talking points or challenges for your industry as a whole?

Regulatory clarity: The CLARITY Act was blocked in the Senate [in September], so US market structure rules are on hold. The groundwork is laid, with the GENIUS Act and MiCA settling how a compliant issuer looks, but it’s still early.

Compliance: The second is getting compliance to move with the payment. Today a receiving institution re-checks a customer the sending institution already verified, so money that settles in seconds still takes days to clear. Solving that is more of a coordination problem than a technical one, and whoever gets it right unlocks a lot of speed that’s already sitting there.

Last-mile settlement: More than 70 countries now run instant domestic payment systems, and stablecoins are the first thing that can link them in real time but where the industry still has to prove itself is the final step into a local bank account or wallet because that is where it varies.

Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: Airwallex and ONE Store Sign MOU to Back Korean Game Dev Expansion
snippet: Airwallex and Korean app marketplace ONE Store have signed an MOU to simplify cross-border payments for Korean game developers going global. The post Airwallex and ONE Store Sign MOU to Back Korean Game Dev Expansion appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Airwallex and ONE Store, South Korea’s leading independent app marketplace, have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore a strategic partnership aimed at reducing the financial complexity facing Korean game developers and publishers as they expand into international markets. The agreement was signed on 15 October in Seoul, with senior representatives from both companies present.

The partnership is framed around combining ONE Store’s domestic gaming distribution network with Airwallex’s cross-border payments infrastructure. Korean developers operating globally routinely encounter fragmented payment landscapes: differing platform fee structures, local payment method requirements and multiple acquiring relationships that add cost and operational overhead before a single player transaction is processed. The two companies say they intend to explore ways to address that friction, though specific products or integration terms have not yet been announced.

The strategic logic

ONE Store occupies a distinctive position in the Korean app economy. As an independent marketplace it sits outside the Google Play and Apple App Store duopoly, and its expansion vehicle, ONE Store Global, signals an ambition to export that model. For Airwallex, the partnership extends its footprint in the gaming vertical, a sector where cross-border payment volumes are high, margin sensitivity is acute and the need to support multiple currencies and local payment methods is structural rather than incidental.

Keun Bin Kim, head of Enterprise for South Korea at Airwallex, noted that Korean developers are building businesses for players around the world and said the partnership is intended to simplify global payment experiences as they reach new audiences. Henry Chang, chief executive of ONE Store, said that as Korean developers increasingly target global markets, working with Airwallex offers an opportunity to reduce the complexity of international payments and operations.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

Airwallex holds more than 85 regulatory licences across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific, which is a meaningful operational asset in a sector where payment acceptance in each new market typically requires a regulated local entity or a licensed partner. For game developers, that breadth matters: a title launching simultaneously in Japan, Germany and Brazil needs locally compliant payment acceptance in each territory, and managing that through a single provider reduces the compliance and treasury overhead considerably.

The broader context is worth noting. South Korea is one of the world’s largest games markets by revenue, and its developers, including globally recognised studios and a deep tier of mid-sized publishers, have accelerated international distribution following the domestic success of titles that have found audiences well beyond the peninsula. Payment infrastructure has historically been a bottleneck: Korean won settlement, hedging costs and the reconciliation burden of multi-currency revenue streams are recurring operational complaints in the sector.

Competition in the cross-border payments space for gaming is active. Several specialist platforms and embedded-finance providers target game developers specifically, and the major global payment processors have built vertical products aimed at this segment. Airwallex’s position is that its regulated infrastructure and multi-currency account architecture offer a more unified operating layer than assembling point solutions per market.

Airwallex has also confirmed it will participate in G-STAR, the Korean games industry trade event scheduled for November, where it plans to engage directly with developers and publishers on the practicalities of global expansion. That appearance will be the first tangible public test of how commercially developed the partnership is beyond the MOU stage.

The MOU represents an intent to explore rather than a concluded commercial agreement, and the announcement contains no committed product roadmap, revenue targets or implementation timeline. Readers should treat the current announcement as a statement of direction.

title: CarbonAI Raises $12m to Automate CRE Lending Underwriting
snippet: The agentic AI platform for commercial real estate lending closed a Cowboy Ventures-led round six months after reaching seven-figure contracted revenue. The post CarbonAI Raises $12m to Automate CRE Lending Underwriting appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
CarbonAI has closed a $12 million funding round led by Cowboy Ventures, with participation from Timber Grove Ventures, Bling Capital, and Max Ventures. The New York-based company builds AI agents that automate the analytical work of commercial real estate lending, covering underwriting, due diligence, investment memo drafting, and post-close loan surveillance.

The round comes roughly six months after CarbonAI launched its first product suite and, the company says, after reaching seven figures in contracted annual revenue. Named customers include debt funds, mortgage REITs, agency multifamily lenders, and publicly traded financial institutions, though CarbonAI has not disclosed individual client names beyond a reference from Greystone co-president Mordecai Rosenberg, who cited the platform’s due diligence automation.

The problem CarbonAI is addressing

Jeff Saul, co-founder and CEO at CarbonAI

The commercial real estate lending market presents a structural automation gap that the founders argue justifies a purpose-built, vertical AI approach. According to the Mortgage Bankers Association, $875 billion in commercial mortgages mature in 2026 alone, compressing lender timelines at a moment when interest rate pressures are forcing more borrowers to seek restructuring or refinancing. CRE lending teams collectively spend an estimated $50 billion per year on underwriting and loan monitoring, much of it still performed on spreadsheets and through manual document review.

Josh Kaufman, co-founder and COO at CarbonAI

CarbonAI’s agents extract and structure data from rent rolls, leases, financial statements, and legal documents, then autonomously produce underwriting models and flag risks, with every output linked to its source document. The system also handles continuous post-close monitoring rather than the traditional quarterly manual review cycle. Co-founder and chief executive Jeff Saul said the tool was designed to handle work end to end, rather than requiring lenders to prompt it through each step: “Lenders don’t need another chat window that they have to coach through every step. They need agents that already know the job, do it end to end consistently, and show their work.”

The founders bring direct domain credibility. Saul and co-founder Josh Kaufman both began their careers underwriting CRE loans at Starwood Capital, Morgan Stanley, and Guggenheim, before building Nativ, a CRE deal management platform they grew to serve more than 30 lenders across $300 billion in assets under management before selling it to Built, a construction finance software company.

Market context and competitive positioning

The vertical AI for financial services origination is becoming a well-funded category. Generic large language model tools have shown limited traction in highly structured, document-intensive workflows where error margins are narrow and auditability is a regulatory requirement. CarbonAI’s design choice to maintain a full audit trail back to the source document on every figure is directly relevant to the internal credit governance standards that regulated lenders and publicly traded institutions must satisfy.

Several competitors are pursuing adjacent positions in automated CRE workflows, including established data and analytics vendors that have added AI layers and a cohort of newer vertical AI firms targeting either the origination or the surveillance leg of the process. CarbonAI’s differentiation rests on covering the full loan lifecycle in a single system and on the founders’ operator pedigree, which Cowboy Ventures partner Caroline Duffy cited as a primary factor in the investment decision.

The reference from Greystone, one of the larger agency multifamily lenders in the US, adds credible early validation. The metrics to watch going forward are customer retention, revenue growth rate, and whether the company pursues regulated activities that would require additional licensing as its agents take on more autonomous decision-adjacent functions in the lending workflow.
