title: TransferGo and UNITED24 Launch Ukraine Student Charity Transfer Campaign
snippet: TransferGo is donating 0.2% of every transfer to a Ukrainian IBAN to UNITED24's education fund until 29 October. The post TransferGo and UNITED24 Launch Ukraine Student Charity Transfer Campaign appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TransferGo has launched a time-limited charitable campaign with UNITED24, the Ukrainian government’s official fundraising platform, under the banner “Transfers That Unite”. Until 29 October 2026, the remittance company will contribute an additional 0.2% of every transfer sent to a Ukrainian IBAN to UNITED24’s Education and Science programme, at no extra cost to the sender.

The campaign is framed around supporting Ukrainian students enrolled at domestic colleges, a population that has faced sustained disruption since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The BigThings 2.0 event

To mark the initiative, TransferGo held its BigThings 2.0 event in Warsaw on 10 October, drawing nearly 150 attendees, including more than 100 Ukrainian content creators based across Poland. Influencers travelled from Krakow, Poznan, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Lublin and Szczecin for an event the company described as combining community networking with practical guidance on growing digital audiences.

The guest of honour was Ukrainian singer Kateryna Pavlenko, known professionally as MONOKATE, who spoke about the cultural value of Ukrainian-language content and performed a short acoustic set. Valentyna Kuzmin, Vice Consul of the Consulate General of Ukraine in Krakow, also attended. The format echoed TransferGo’s previous community events: a first BigThings gathering in Warsaw in 2025 and a TRUE INFLUENCE event for Ukrainian creators held in Prague this spring.

Krzysztof Szatecki, Brand and Demand Director at TransferGo, said: “Ukrainian creators abroad have become some of the strongest voices keeping Ukraine’s story alive, and BigThings 2.0 was our way of bringing those voices into one room. Every transfer home is already an act of care for family, and with Transfers That Unite, we’re making sure that it also helps the next generation of Ukrainian professionals finish their studies.”

Market and regulatory context

Remittance corridors to Ukraine have been a significant commercial focus for cross-border payment providers since 2022. Ukraine became one of the world’s largest remittance-receiving economies as its diaspora expanded, and several fintech firms have competed for a share of the Polish-to-Ukraine corridor in particular. TransferGo, which says it serves more than nine million customers across 160 countries and has operated for 14 years, counts the Ukrainian diaspora as a core demographic.

The “Transfers That Unite” mechanism, in which a fraction of a commercial transaction fee is redirected to a charitable fund, is an established model in the remittance sector. It sidesteps the friction of asking senders to make a separate donation while generating measurable social impact data that can be used in brand positioning. The 0.2% contribution rate is modest on individual transactions but can aggregate meaningfully across a high-volume corridor.

UNITED24, launched by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in May 2022, reported cumulative fundraising of more than $3.9 billion from donors in over 145 countries as of the date of the release. The platform operates across several programme areas; the Education and Science strand is the recipient of this campaign’s proceeds.

For TransferGo, the initiative also serves as a community-building exercise among diaspora influencers, a distribution channel for brand awareness in a segment where trust and peer recommendation matter more than traditional advertising. The effectiveness of that channel will depend on how actively the creator network promotes the campaign before the 29 October close date.

fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

Only through partnership can we deliver the system-wide response needed to protect market integrity. And that is the foundation necessary so innovation can flourish, productivity can rise and growth can endure.

The UK is incredibly well placed to harness the power of new technology. The existing strength of this sector gives us a genuine head start.

If we can harness technological progress – if we continue to lead – financial services can place the UK at the forefront of this new era of innovation.

As regulators, we are committed to creating the conditions for you to do that.

Together, we can build a future that the whole country will be proud of…

title: NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK Join CFIT Financial Inclusion Coalition
snippet: Three major UK banks have backed CFIT's coalition to develop a Supported Payments framework for people who need help managing money without ceding full The post NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK Join CFIT Financial Inclusion Coalition appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK have confirmed participation in the Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology‘s Financial Inclusion Coalition, announced on 15 October 2026. The coalition is developing a Supported Payments framework intended to create a legally recognised middle ground between full financial independence and formal arrangements such as Lasting Power of Attorney or deputyship.

The move follows HM Treasury‘s Economic Secretary welcoming the initiative at the Fintech as a Force for Good conference in London the previous week, underlining a degree of government alignment that CFIT has been careful to cultivate since receiving Treasury funding to take the project forward.

From grassroots campaign to institutional programme

The coalition’s origins lie in Project Nemo, a not-for-profit founded by Joanne Dewar and Kris Foster that spent more than two years building the evidence base for disability inclusion in financial services. Nationwide led a significant research publication through that initiative, identifying a structural gap: for people with learning disabilities or other conditions requiring assistance with day-to-day spending, the current system offers no practical midpoint. The choice, in effect, is between informal workarounds such as sharing cards, PINs and online banking credentials, or triggering disproportionately heavy legal arrangements designed for more serious incapacity.

CFIT launched the coalition formally at Money20/20 Europe in June 2026, and the addition of three of the UK’s largest retail banks gives it the institutional weight needed to move from research into implementation.

Anna Wallace, chief executive of CFIT, said: “For too many people, getting help to manage their money still means giving up more control than they should have to. Tackling that challenge requires coordinated action across the industry. CFIT is here to do exactly that: marshal the expertise, commitment and resources needed to move beyond recognising the problem to developing and testing practical solutions that deliver meaningful change.”

What the framework will do and when

Through the remainder of 2026, coalition participants will run focused sprints across two workstreams. The first is a Trust and Consent Framework, covering how individuals could appoint a trusted third party to assist with payments without a formal Power of Attorney, along with consent and permissioning models, liability considerations and regulatory alignment. The second workstream is a proof-of-concept pilot, potentially leveraging open banking infrastructure, to test supported payment journeys in real-world environments with consumers, carers and financial institutions. People with lived experience will be involved directly in designing and testing the proposed customer journey.

An interim report setting out the coalition’s initial findings and governance framework is expected before the end of the year. That will feed into a second phase focused on building and testing a minimum viable product for Supported Payments.

Regulatory and market context

The initiative sits within a broader UK push to make consumer financial services more inclusive. HM Treasury’s Financial Inclusion Strategy has previously cited the barriers faced by disabled consumers, and the FCA‘s Consumer Duty, which came into full force in 2023, places explicit obligations on firms to deliver good outcomes for customers in vulnerable circumstances. A Supported Payments framework would give banks a structured, regulated mechanism to meet those obligations rather than relying on informal accommodations that can expose both customer and institution to risk.

The open banking angle is worth watching. Using Payment Initiation Services or Account Information Services under the existing PSD2-derived framework in the UK could allow a trusted third party to initiate or oversee payments on behalf of a customer without requiring full account access, potentially resolving some of the consent and liability questions the coalition is working through. Whether that technical path proves sufficient, or whether primary legislation will be needed to establish the liability framework for trusted third parties, is likely to be a central question in the interim report.

title: Venmo results lift PayPal
snippet: The digital payments processor is benefiting from its peer-to-peer payment tool business after cutting 2,000 employee jobs.
fullText:
Digital payments pioneer PayPal Holdings sought to allay fears about slowing growth during an earnings report Tuesday by pointing to improvements for its peer-to-peer brand Venmo and diversification of revenue streams. 

The company’s third-quarter earnings report showed mid-teen growth for Venmo transaction volume helped lift overall results, buffering slower single-digit growth at its legacy checkout brand. The number of Venmo debit card holders jumped by about 55% to 6.7 million monthly active accounts, including 1.6 million who used it for the first time in the quarter, PayPal CEO Enrique Lores said during a conference call with analysts to discuss the results.

“We are building on the strength of the Venmo brand to broaden adoption of financial services, deepen customer relationships and increase (average revenue per account),” Lores told analysts during the company’s conference call.

Lores, who took the top post in March, has sought to jump-start growth and profitability at the early innovator in digital payments as the field of fintech competitors mushrooms. He’s the third person to hold the job in as many years as the company has struggled with stagnating growth amid volatile economic conditions and rising competition.

To bolster the bottom line, the company embarked this year on reducing management layers and cutting its headcount. It has eliminated some 2,000 jobs, as it adds more artificial intelligence tools to automate some parts of the operation, Lores told analysts. 

PayPal sells services to merchants, including retailers and other merchants, as well as consumers, making it one of the few payments players to have a two-sided business.

The company acquired Venmo in 2013 when it purchased the Braintree business, which provides processing services to large companies. Since then, PayPal leaders have been at a loss to better monetize the Venmo brand despite its P2P popularity with a younger generation of consumers. It has offered a Venmo debit card since at least 2018.

Instigating growth for Venmo has been a key goal for the company for years, especially given the flagging growth at the legacy checkout PayPal brand. Former CEOs Dan Schulman and Alex Chriss were hard pressed to offset the slowing momentum at PayPal as macroeconomic factors, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the tariff war under President Donald Trump, put a damper on demand.

The company’s Venmo credit card, introduced in 2020, hasn’t fared as well as the new debit card, but the company pivoted on that offering early this month. PayPal revamped the credit card’s rewards program to offer up to 4% cash back on certain dining and entertainment transactions, according to an Oct. 5 press release. That includes a bump in rewards when the card holder uses it to split the payment of a purchase.

With the company’s stock having dropped 76% during the past five years, Lores has sought to protect the business from low-ball bids. Under his leadership, the company in July reportedly rejected an offer from the younger processor juggernaut Stripe, backed by private equity investor Advent International.

While the Venmo business is helping drive the Lores quest for profitable growth, the increase in volume for the company’s legacy PayPal branded checkout business has remained “relatively stable” at 1% to 2% growth over the past four quarters, he said.

Meanwhile, the CEO is trying to diversify the company’s revenue, also by building demand for financial services, like its buy now, pay later offering and seeking to build demand in Europe where the company is rolling out services it has begun to scale in the U.S. 

“While there is more work to do, we're encouraged by the improvement relative to the market, continued momentum in the U.S., and strength in BNPL and Pay with Venmo,” Enrique told analysts on the call. “These results show that our financial performance is increasingly coming from multiple parts of the business.”

Third-quarter net income sunk 14% to $1.07 billion even as revenue edged up 2% to $8.6 billion and overall payments volume climbed 6% compared with the year-earlier quarter, according to the San Jose, California-based company’s earnings release.

Analysts had a tepid reaction to the results. The report was “mixed,” RBC analysts told their investment clients, noting the company fell short of analysts’ revenue projections, but offered some better profit figures and increased the outlook for the full year. TD Cowen analysts told clients the net result of the earnings report was “ok,” with “no surprises” in the low bar set by the company’s turnaround plan.  

PayPal plans to continue investing in more growth, directing some of the $1.5 billion in savings it expects over several years to new efforts to scale the parts of the business where it’s seeing successes. Those investments will temper profits to some degree, so the company’s executives sought to temper expectations on the call with the analysts who counsel investors.

“We are still early in these changes,” Lores told analysts. “This is a multi-year transformation, and there is much more work to do, but the progress we are seeing reinforces our conviction in the strategy.”

PayPal’s chief financial officer, Jamie Miller, underscored that sentiment in delving into the company’s financial results.

“The savings are creating capacity to self-fund more of our growth investments, such as improving the consumer experience, strengthening merchant presentment, and building and scaling our financial services products,” Miller said on the call. “As we learn what's working, we're being deliberate about where we invest more and where we pull back.”

She also attempted to make sure investors understand the changes will take time.

“We're really encouraged by the results we're seeing, but it's early, and we've got more work to do,” Miller said. “In the U.S. in particular, we saw nice sequential growth over the past few quarters in U.S. branded checkout (total processing volume) growth, so we're seeing good signs, but we also don't want to get ahead of ourselves, she said, noting a three-year “time horizon” for reviving the PayPal branded checkout business.

fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

title: Elavon pursues Paze, agentic commerce
snippet: Mobile wallet Paze is “ready to do pilots,” said Wally Mlynarski, CEO of the U.S. Bank subsidiary.
fullText:
As banking and payments players grapple with the rise of artificial intelligence agents, Elavon CEO Wally Mlynarski points to two lessons that influence his agentic commerce considerations.

The first relates to fraud. Since the introduction of e-commerce, “we've been chasing and trying to stamp out fraud for 25 years, and we’ve made all the mistakes,” Mlynarski said of the industry.

That includes card verification value codes, Payment Card Industry data security standards and keyed entry transactions, all designed to manage risk, said Mlynarski, chief executive of U.S. Bank subsidiary Elavon, an Atlanta-based merchant payment services provider.

“We could go screw that up again with agentic commerce, or we can actually focus on safety and soundness,” Mlynarski said during an interview at last week’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. 

Big-bank CEOs such as JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon and PNC’s Bill Demchak have expressed liability concerns with AI agents acting on behalf of customers.

The second lesson relates to costs and benefits. The mobile wallet wars of the 2010s – featuring Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and, eventually, the big banks’ response, Paze – were about making the economics work, Mlynarski said. And that proved difficult. 

Wally Mlynarski

Permission granted by U.S. Bank

“Entering agents into the flow of the consumer, the merchant, the acquirer, the issuing bank, and the networks, and now trying to add economics here to make this work, or take away economics from somebody in that chain, is going to be a challenge,” Mlynarski said.  

To that end, he’s focused on understanding the value consumers are being offered, and prioritizing trust and safety and soundness, as agentic technology takes off while standards and protocols are being sorted out. 

Meta Platforms has added Stripe’s Link digital wallet to facilitate payments by its personal AI agent Muse; consumers have also started using Instinct and OpenAI’s dots. 

Such launches and pilots are “not necessarily thinking about all the safety and soundness in there,” Mlynarski said, contrasting those approaches with bank-driven efforts.

Mlynarski returned to Elavon this year after a stint at Bank of America, where he led merchant services and receivables. He said he helped shape Early Warning Services’ Paze mobile wallet, which can work within agentic commerce and address agent hallucination issues, among other things.

Paze is “ready to do pilots,” Mlynarski said. Early Warning Services is owned by seven large U.S. banks, including U.S. Bank. 

“We can create an ecosystem that does make this successful. And if we do that right and don't race into it too quickly, consumers will have a good experience. Merchants will have a good experience. Issuers will have a good experience. And then we'll see scale,” he said. 

“If we race into it and do it incorrectly,” he said, “consumers are going to be harmed.”

Mlynarski also sees his business as an accelerator for Minneapolis-based U.S. Bank’s deposits and lending growth. That includes enabling Elavon’s merchant customers to offer buy now, pay later, and providing capital for small-business clients’ liquidity needs. 

“If you think about how we position and work with our clients to bring in deposits to the bank – obviously, to keep those deposits, we have to do the full cycle,” he said. “We have to be able to do the payments portion of that, on the back end. … But if I can solve the front-end receivables side and bring in the mass volume of our retail clients or our lodging, airlines, etc., I can actually bring in deposits.” 

Weaving U.S. Bank’s capabilities and services into what Elavon offers its merchant customers is an ongoing pursuit, he indicated. 

As U.S. Bank chases growth in the small-business segment, bundling services can help the lender stand out as it seeks scale, CFO John Stern said this month. 

“More and more, my business is moving into software,” Mlynarski said. 

Clients’ point-of-sale and enterprise resource planning systems are their “lifeblood,” so “the more we can embed the bank into those solutions, we can bring lending to them when they need it, we can bring a receivables solution or other things that they might need to manage the business,” he said.

Increasingly, that includes security solutions, enabling small businesses with antivirus software, he noted. 

“We are the game of connections,” he said. “We drive all those connections together to simplify that, to package that, so the business doesn’t have to go solve that.”

title: Liability looms over AI shopping
snippet: Some banks and other payment players lament how agentic commerce has steamrolled ahead without “rules of the road” for liability issues.
fullText:
The red coat still bothers Early Warning Services CEO Cameron Fowler.

His son purchased a new red coat, in the wrong size as it turned out, using social media company Meta Platforms’ Muse personal agent, Fowler recalled last week in an interview.

“I don’t know why you want a red coat, but more a red coat that doesn’t fit you and … who’s liable for that?” Fowler said on Oct. 19, recounting the conversation with his son, one of “the early 20-year-olds in my house who are on the front foot” of agentic-powered shopping.

For Fowler, the ill-fitting red coat symbolizes an array of issues confronting the industry in a new era of agentic payments as consumers direct their personal agents to shop for them. The formulation of corporate policies and federal legislation to address topics such as liability, data access and consumer intent has sorely lagged the pace of agent technology, he said on the sidelines of the annual Money20/20 financial technology conference.

“What do you need to have in place to ensure that the least-informed consumer actually understands the commitments they’re making, and that we are very clear on the relationship between human and authorization,” said Fowler, a former BMO Financial Group banker who leads EWS. “That’s where the rubber meets the road.”

With consumers beginning to tap artificial intelligence agents to shop and make payments, the banking industry is increasingly edgy about risks associated with bot traffic inside customers’ accounts. Early Warning Services, parent of the Zelle payment service and Paze digital wallet, is owned by seven large U.S. banks.

Some bank executives are alarmed and incensed by the prospect of machines making payments without liability measures in place, given what they consider the inherent risks. 

The CEO of PNC Financial Services Group, William “Bill” Demchak, railed against tech companies for barreling into agentic transactions without heeding the perils during his Oct. 19 appearance at the Money20/20 conference.

“There’d have to be a massive liability shift that these guys took on the liability associated with breaking all the crap they’re about to break,” he said. “They’re kids in a room with a new toy, and they’re messing around with money … this isn’t a game,” Demchak said. “This isn’t like normal technology where you’re allowed to break stuff and figure it out later. You’re messing with people’s lives. It’s money.” 

Meta’s Muse agent

Fears about the fast pace of agentic commerce were sparked when Meta Platforms released its Muse personal agent in the U.S. and Canada in September. 

Agentic commerce “started going vertical” that same month, Stripe President John Collison said in a podcast discussion earlier this month. Meta said last week that shopping is the top task among Muse’s 10 million early users. Beyond the banks’ agentic blocks, retail giant Amazon has also refused Meta’s agent entry to its shopping sites.

A detailed audit trail for agentic transactions is “extremely crucial” to enable responsible commerce, card network Visa’s head of strategic financial institution and fintech partnerships, Kaitlan Moran, said Oct. 20 at a Money20/20 panel on agentic commerce.

“From our perspective, the really important thing is to make sure that we’re creating that trust layer and providing that enhanced context and data and information to all of the parties in the ecosystem,” Moran said. 

Standards are still under development and “we don’t have case law on liability,” said John Piazza, product lead for digital payment processor Stripe’s card issuing business, and an adjunct professor at Northwestern University’s Pritzker School of Law. Stripe’s Link digital wallet helps to enable payments by the Muse agent.

“There’s still a lot of macro questions,” he said, speaking on the same panel with Moran, about agent-driven payments.

New rules of the payment road 

In the “traditional” four-party payment model of cardholders, merchants, issuers and acquirers, networks influence behavior through interchange rates and chargeback rules, said Andrew Lambert, the head of product for Cross River Bank, a Fort Lee, New Jersey-based banking-as-a-service provider.

A merchant that offered a network more transaction data might benefit from a lower interchange cost or could shift liability on a given transaction by demonstrating tighter security measures, Lambert said, speaking on the same panel as the Stripe and Visa executives.

“When you’re talking about an agent platform that sits outside of that ecosystem, those levers don’t work anymore, and I think that’s the thing that I find the most perplexing,” Lambert said. Card networks should provide “more guidance around rules of the road” for agentic transactions, he added.

Wells Fargo, the fourth-largest U.S. bank by assets, is warning customers that they might be liable for agents’ errors if they share their account details. “Just like humans, AI can make mistakes,” the bank wrote in an Oct. 2 customer email. “If you give an AI tool your username and password, you may be liable for any mistakes made by the AI tool.”

Proliferating protocols

The major card networks, including Visa, Mastercard and American Express, have adopted different protocols for how agents should transact. Visa’s “trusted agent” approach, for example, involves a directory of known agents, while Mastercard’s “agent pay” adopts an authorization process to tokenize payment credentials for agents’ access.

Tech titans Google and Stripe, joined by payment processors, have also introduced agentic protocols to help forge operational standards for these new shopping bots. 

Some of the new infrastructure hasn’t been rolled out yet, which has prompted concerns about liability and other issues, Google’s vice president and general manager of payments, Stavan Parikh, said Monday in an interview.

“What has happened in the ecosystem so far is not leveraging what the networks have fully built out,” he said. “But I expect in the coming weeks and months we will see people moving to more of these standardized infrastructures.”

Two large players in the payments industry — American Express and Stripe – have announced consumer purchase protection policies aimed at agentic transactions. 

Among other terms, Amex’s rules require that the cardholder’s agent be registered with the company. If a purchase goes awry, the purchaser must send a “purchase intent” document to help prove that a particular transaction deviated from the consumer’s intent. Stripe’s plan covers purchases in the U.S. made through Link, with extensive caveats in the user terms about monitoring the agent’s activity.

Still, limited rules from two companies hardly suffice for transactions that could reach into the trillions over time, industrywide, Fowler said.

“I’m sure there are lots of people who are orchestrating wonderful transactions, but here we’re talking about hundreds and hundreds of millions of consumers who have no idea how powerful the thing is and may not have been fully educated on the risks that they’re taking, and that’s not acceptable,” Fowler said.

“At the end of the day, was there a human that authorized (a transaction), and if so, what's the liability? If not, what's the liability? I think that that needs to be in place for the industry, not for a couple of the players.”

title: Visa adapts to tech innovations
snippet: The card network’s fiscal 2026 results show it’s reaching beyond legacy payments paths to incorporate new technologies, offer new services and extend its global reach with more partners.
fullText:
Visa is intent on demonstrating that it can adapt to a changing world, despite naysayers who earlier this year questioned whether it would be able to compete with new technologies.

In presenting the company’s fiscal full-year results Tuesday, Visa’s CEO, Ryan McInerney, rattled off a list of accomplishments for the year, including record net revenue of $46 billion that grew at the fastest rate in 15 years, excluding leaps after the COVID-19 pandemic and due to acquisitions.

All of which led to the San Francisco-based company reporting what McInerney called “milestone” results for the fiscal year 2026 that ended on Sept. 30. 

“In 2026, we also demonstrated that whenever technology changes commerce, we move with it,” McInerney said, gloating on a webcast over the results. “We anticipate what's next, and we enable its growth as the leading hyperscaler of payments globally.”

The company’s stock flagged earlier this year as analysts and investors worried that the largest U.S. card network company might not be able to adapt to technological changes, including stablecoins and agentic commerce, reshaping the payments industry. Concerns have also increased as fintech startups, such as Stripe and Adyen, gather momentum. 

But Visa’s stock soared Wednesday, crossing $400 a share for an all-time high. The increase came after Visa reported fourth-quarter net income rose 18% to $6 billion, pushing up the full-year profit 17% to $23.5 billion, according to a Tuesday press release. 

Analysts were quick to praise the financial results, with those at Bank of America citing Visa’s “broad based strength” and those at TD Cowen saying the report “demonstrated the strength of the franchise across core payments.” 

Visa’s revenue increase for the fiscal year, including a 13% jump for the fourth quarter over the year-ago period to $12 billion, occurred as the company processed 9% more transactions, 281 billion, over last year and as cross-border activity jumped 12%, McInerney said. Overall payments volume rose 9%, with 12% commercial payments volume growth outstripping consumer payment growth. 

The results showed how Visa is creating a portfolio of services beyond its traditional card payment rails. Specifically, McInerney pointed to software services sold to corporate clients increasing 19% and its value-added services consulting revenue rising 30% over fiscal 2025. Collectively, those two revenue streams made up about 40% of the company’s overall revenue.

McInerney touted Visa’s expansion by way of new partners, pointing to consulting services that include a new investment in Overwatch Data, a firm that provides threat intelligence services and its recent acquisition of fraud prevention services company Biocatch; the company’s work with Shopify and Anthropic on agentic commerce; and its support for five stablecoins and 10 blockchain projects around the world.

The company is also scaling in new regions of the world, handling its first transaction in Syria in over a decade during the year and Latin America accounting for about one-fifth of its 5.2 billion payment credentials issued worldwide. 

Tap-to-pay, tap-to-phone, peer-to-peer payments and remittances carried on its Visa Direct network are all among the ways in which Visa is seeking to keep its dominant grasp on payments around the world. 

Analysts on the webcast were particularly interested in Visa’s outlook for agentic commerce, the innovation in which shopping and payments are driven by artificial intelligence agents. While McInerney was eager to support the potential of that new technology to lift the business, he also cautioned that the agentic era is in a nascent stage, with work still being done to allow its safe and efficient use.

Some banks and online retail behemoth Amazon have made moves to block AI agents from operating on their systems.

“We want to make sure that there's a clear path to resolution in the event of a problem, so disputes, rules, and processes and things like that,” McInerney said. “And then finally, we want to make sure that this all works securely everywhere in the world for billions of users at scale.”

With consumers and businesses seeking payments security in a new era of technological innovations, McInerney contends they will reach for a brand name they know.

“As I look ahead to 2027, one thing is clear: trust is the next growth vector for Visa,” the CEO said. “Trust fuels everything we do at Visa every day, and trust will fuel our future.”

title: Fed loses debit card cap appeal
snippet: The Federal Reserve’s debit card interchange rule doesn’t follow the intent of Congress in setting a limit for swipe fees, an appellate court ruled Monday.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve has improperly determined rules for setting a fee cap on debit card transactions, a federal appeals court ruled Monday in vacating the central bank’s current 21-cent fee limit.

The decision by a three-judge panel of the Eighth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals – which backed a lower court ruling from last year – represented a victory for merchants that have battled payment card swipe fees for years.

Plaintiffs alleged that the Federal Reserve System Board of Governors should have set a debit card interchange standard that considers only an issuer’s marginal costs for a transaction, not the fixed expenses that come with its overall business. Any costs “not specific to a particular electronic debit transaction” shouldn’t be used by the Fed to set the debit fee cap, the court found in reading the statute.

That type of cost distinction within the Fed’s Regulation II rules is what Congress intended in 2010 when it added the Durbin Amendment to the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, the St. Louis-based appeals court said.

The Fed’s current debit card fee structure includes far more than the marginal cost for each debit transaction, and disregards Congress’ intent when it enacted the amendment, the appeals court panel wrote in its ruling. 

The Fed’s rate cap included banks’ “fixed costs related to authorization, clearance, and settlement,” along with network processing fees, costs for fraud prevention and for losses due to fraud, the appeals court said. 

“It does not take much detective work to figure out that the Federal Reserve ‘shall . . . consider’ marginal costs in setting debit-card interchange fees, but not fixed costs,” the judges wrote. “No matter how much some banks and payment networks disagree with approaching the problem this way, the Federal Reserve does not get to revise Congress’s work.”

“Make no mistake, debit-card interchange fees do not have to exactly match marginal cost,” the court added. “The word ‘proportional,’ after all, does not require perfection. The Federal Reserve is free to use a proxy, perhaps even average variable cost, if it bears a ‘reasonable’ relationship to the marginal costs incurred by cardholder banks in processing debit-card transactions.”

As part of Regulation II, the Fed capped debit card swipe fees in 2011 at 21 cents, plus 0.05% of the value of the debit transaction, in addition to allowing a one-cent fraud-prevention add-on.

The cap is subject to revision every two years, and applies only to banks and financial institutions that have $10 billion or more in deposits. The Fed proposed in October 2023 to change the cap for the first time, suggesting the base debit fee rate be lowered by about 30% to 14.4 cents. The Fed has not moved forward since then.

A Fed spokesperson said the agency had no comment on the ruling or the status of its 2023 fee proposal.

The Fed “must sort the costs into those that are transaction-specific and those that are not,” the appeals panel wrote. “Not just pick a number and hope it is close enough for government work.”

The lawsuit dates to April 2021, when Corner Post, a truck stop and convenience store in Watford City, North Dakota, filed a lawsuit against the Fed seeking to lower its debit card transaction costs.

U.S. District Judge Daniel Traynor in North Dakota struck down the Fed board’s fee regulations in August 2025, leading to the appeal. Traynor has since joined the Eighth Circuit court after the Senate confirmed him in July. He was not on the three-judge panel that ruled on the Fed’s appeal.

The Merchants Payments Coalition hailed the ruling in a press release as a win for both merchants and consumers.

“Two courts have now agreed that the current rate lets banks collect billions of dollars a year more from stores and their customers than the law ever meant for them to have — far more than it takes to cover their costs and earn a healthy profit,” Doug Kantor, who is general counsel for the National Association of Convenience Stores, said in the press release.

Kantor, who also sits on the coalition’s executive committee, called for the Fed to replace its debit-fee rule “with one that complies with the law and takes some of the upward pressure off the prices shoppers pay every day.” NACS was among numerous merchant and banking groups that filed amicus briefs with the appeals court.

Bank and payment groups, including the American Bankers Association, America’s Credit Unions and the Electronic Payments Coalition, said in a joint statment Monday they were “deeply disappointed” by the 8th Circuit’s decision.

“For more than a decade, corporate megastores have pocketed billions from the Durbin Amendment while ignoring promises to lower prices for consumers,” said the statement from six groups. “Now, they want to pay even less for the very payment system they rely on every day, leaving banks, credit unions and consumers to shoulder the costs.”

The trade groups also pointed to a second case over debit card fees pending in the Sixth Circuit, Linney’s Pizza vs. Federal Reserve, in which a federal court in the Eastern District of Kentucky last year found in favor of the Fed’s rule.

“It’s important to remember that this decision is not the last word on these issues,” the bank groups said in their statement.

fullText:
On 15 October 2026, ePayments Systems Limited (EPS) entered special administration. Mark Boast and Allister Manson of Opus Restructuring LLP (Opus) have been appointed as joint special administrators. 

  

            						

EPS is authorised by the FCA to issue e-money under the Electronic Money Regulations 2011 (EMRs).

See details on the Financial Services Register.

Who to contact

The special administrators are responsible for managing customer claims against the firm and returning funds to customers where possible.

If you have any questions about the administration process, please contact the special administrators:

Email: [email protected]

Website: opusllp.com

As the firm continues to be authorised by us, we will engage with the special administrators and seek the best outcome for customers. 

          

        

Information for EPS customers

    

      

      						What is special administration?
			
    

    

						

The Payment and Electronic Money Institution Insolvency Regulations 2021 introduced a special administration regime for payment and e-money institutions.

This is similar to an ordinary administration, with additional objectives of returning customer funds as soon as reasonably practicable and ensuring timely engagement with payment systems operators and the authorities, including the FCA.

			

  

      

      						What should I do if I have money with EPS?
			
    

    

						

If you’re concerned or have any questions, contact the special administrators for help or updates.  

Email: [email protected]

The special administrators will gather information from creditors and customers about payments made to, or owed by, EPS and will provide more information on how to make a claim in due course.  

Customers can also contact our Consumer Helpline for more information. 

			

  

      

      						Is the FCA overseeing the special administration?
			
    

    

						

The special administrators are now responsible for EPS, but it continues to be FCA authorised and remains subject to our rules.  The special administrators are officers of the court and must comply with insolvency law.

They have statutory objectives, including engaging with relevant authorities such as the FCA and we will continue working with them during the special administration. 

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a third party to get my money back? 
			
    

    

						

If you are approached by a company offering to help you recover your money, you should proceed with caution. 

For most of the firm’s clients, there will be no benefit in involving a third party in making a claim.    

If you have any questions about the special administration process, please contact the special administrators using the contact details above.  

			

  

  

            						

Being alert to scams

All customers should remain alert to the possibility of fraud.

If you are contacted unexpectedly by someone claiming to be from EPS, Opus or the FCA, you should end the call and contact them directly using verified contact details.

Find out more about protecting yourself from scams.

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags
snippet: Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests. A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest. Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research. Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests.

  

            						

A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out.  

The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.

Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest.  

Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research.  

Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. Hype, urgency and fear of missing out can all influence how people invest, so before acting on an opportunity, do your research and make sure it's right for you.'

The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.

Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.

title: FTC, states sue Toast over fees
snippet: The agency and eight states allege that the point-of-sale services provider charges its restaurant clients and their customers hidden fees.
fullText:
The Federal Trade Commission and eight states sued Toast on Thursday, alleging that the point-of-sale company misled restaurant clients and their customers with hidden fees and subscription plans that were difficult to cancel. 

The lawsuit also said that Toast failed to deliver the customer support help that it had pledged, and obscured a 99-cent fee Toast collected from consumers who placed online orders.

“Toast failed to honor a number of its promises and instead imposed hidden fees, unauthorized charges and subscription traps that drained the hard‑earned profits of businesses just trying to serve their customers,” the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection director, Christopher Mufarrige, said Thursday in a press release.

The FTC was joined in the lawsuit by California and attorneys general in seven states: Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Utah.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for Northern California, says that “at least tens of thousands of consumers have complained about these issues to the FTC, online, and directly to Toast.”

Toast said in a press release that it disagreed with the allegations “and will vigorously defend” itself against the claims.

“Toast has been cooperating fully with the FTC's review of this matter since mid-2025 and has engaged in good faith throughout, including efforts to reach a resolution short of litigation,” the company said. “The FTC disregarded the information we provided showing the extent to which our restaurant customers negotiate their contracts. We are prepared to defend our business and fight this unprecedented action through litigation.” 

Boston-based Toast sells hardware and software services, including payment processing, to help restaurants and other merchants handle their sales.

As part of their Toast agreements, restaurants must enroll in auto-renewing subscriptions, with an average cost of $900 monthly, according to the lawsuit. The monthly cost is determined by how many terminals and added services a business chooses to bundle into the subscription, the plaintiffs said.

“Toast customers frequently complain that they have been enrolled in and charged for Toast subscription add-ons without their consent,” the lawsuit says. 

Toast has “used false claims” to entice customers to enroll in subscription services, including an offer of free Toast products under some pricing plans, along with “24/7/365” customer support, according to the lawsuit.

“In fact, none of Toast’s hardware is $0, and Toast customers frequently claim that they cannot get customer support at any hour of the day,” the lawsuit said.

The company has also made it difficult for customers to end their subscriptions, according to the lawsuit.

“The convoluted, multi-step cancellation process instituted by Toast, combined with Toast’s customer support failures, prevents or makes it hard for consumers to cancel their subscriptions, saddling consumers with additional months or even years of unwanted charges,” the government plaintiffs wrote. 

The lawsuit said that Toast’s subscription cancellation process is “nonintuitive, time-consuming, far from simple, and requires the involvement and cooperation of multiple teams within Toast.”

For those who successfully ended their Toast accounts, “in many instances, Toast has hit them with unexpected high-dollar early termination fees or continued to charge them for subscription services without consent,” the lawsuit says.

The lawsuit also said that Toast is collecting obscured fees from restaurant patrons who order online.

Since June 2023, Toast has collected a 99-cent fee from diners using online digital sales channels for orders above $10, beyond other fees it charged restaurants, according to the lawsuit. The company began testing this fee in some locations in September 2021, according to the lawsuit.

“Nowhere did Toast state that it, not local restaurants, would keep the fee,” the plaintiffs said. “Instead, Toast used language obscuring that it was the primary or sole beneficiary of the fee.”

The lawsuit alleges that Toast violated the FTC Act and the 2010 Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, along with the states’ consumer protection and unfair and deceptive trade practices laws.

In its press release, Toast said that no court has found that the ROSCA law applies to “negotiated business-to-business agreements, and we don’t believe it applies here.”

Toast is scheduled to report its third-quarter financial results on Tuesday.

title: Will ditching the ‘honor all cards’ rule matter?
snippet: Visa and Mastercard agreed to drop the standard in settling litigation with merchants, but the concession may not be much of a victory.
fullText:
A legal settlement ending 20 years of litigation by merchants against Visa and Mastercard includes a concession by the card networks that may not ultimately matter much.

The proposed pact, which still awaits a federal judge’s final approval, would eliminate the longstanding rule that forces merchants to agree to accept all Visa cards if they accept one, and similarly accept all Mastercards if they accept any. The rule means merchants must take the networks’ premium cards, for which they pay higher interchange fees, alongside more standard cards, including debit cards, with lower fees.

The rule change would theoretically let restaurants, retailers or other businesses accept some Visa or Mastercard cards, but not others. It would also provide more leeway for imposing surcharges when the more expensive cards are put on the counter by consumers.

But some merchants aren’t impressed. They oppose the legal settlement offered last year by lawyers for the two sides, saying the agreement falls short of expectations, and that eliminating the “honor all cards” rule would essentially be meaningless.

The CEO of American Express seems to agree with them. When Amex CEO Stephen Squeri was asked to comment on his rivals’ agreement to ditch the rule during a webcast with analysts to discuss that company’s recent third-quarter results, he said as much.

"Good luck,” was Squeri’s knee-jerk response on Friday. 

He presumably was directing that comment to merchants, who he knows would be hard-pressed to decline Visa or Mastercard cards. “It's going to be really hard, I think, for people to differentiate,” he said, suggesting there will be “consumer outrage” if merchants start rejecting certain cards.

The rule has had a somewhat equalizing effect for acceptance of cards held by elite consumers, who often pay to hold those cards and receive more benefits for doing so, and cards with fewer benefits held by consumers not interested in annual card fees. 

Amex has always been in a league of its own, with many high-income cardholder customers who are willing to pay for the privilege of receiving more perks. It’s not a party to the litigation, but Squeri’s comments are telling.

The upshot is: There's not much incentive for merchants to start discriminating between the cards they’re willing to accept. In fact, there’s a big downside, for two key reasons. 

First, as Squeri suggested, it’s a bad experience for consumers. Dan Stiel, a former card industry executive who now advises merchants on payments, shares that view. 

The last thing a retailer wants is consumers digging through their wallets in the checkout line looking for a particular card that a store clerk may or may not recognize as an acceptable card, while other customers watch and wait, explained Stiel, whose Abetica Studios firm is based in Palm Springs, California. 

“You want to create a convenient, hassle-free way to pay for your customers,” Stiel said in an interview Wednesday.

To the extent merchants make it difficult for their customers to pay, they stand to lose customers, or at least upset them. Neither one of which is good. So the idea that customers will take a liking to using one card at a particular retailer, another card at a restaurant and a third card elsewhere is a non-starter. 

The second reason merchants should be reluctant to turn away customers handing them premium cards is that those sales are typically worth their while, despite the higher fees, Stiel said.

“They are exponentially more profitable than someone who might be using a debit card,” Stiel said, describing a customer who drives into a gas station with an expensive car to buy a tank full of premium gas using an elite credit card compared to a customer with a debit card who doesn’t fill up. “It might be a lower cost for merchants, but the tickets are smaller.”

For many merchants, potentially aggravating high-end customers and losing out on bigger sales because they want to avoid higher fees would seem a short-sighted strategy. By contrast, merchants hoping to gain from a slew of smaller sales attached to lower fees might only be lucrative at extremely high volumes. 

Ultimately, elimination of the “honor all cards” rule is an “empty benefit,” Stiel said. “If the merchant community sees this as a big win, I think they’re going to find themselves deeply disappointed.”

Maybe that’s why Visa and Mastercard were willing to do away with the rule.

title: USDA proposes adding chip and tap-to-pay tech to EBT cards
snippet: The National Grocers Association said the payment technologies, which are currently available in nearly a dozen states, can help reduce SNAP fraud.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The National Grocers Association said the payment technologies, which are currently available in nearly a dozen states, can help reduce SNAP fraud.

        

            

        Published Oct. 27, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                A store displays a sign accepting Electronic Benefits Transfer cards for SNAP purchases for groceries on Oct. 30, 2025, in New York City.
            
        
            Spencer Platt via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

 
    

First published on

    

    

                    

Dive Brief:

The Department of Agriculture proposed a rule that would require all states to issue SNAP EBT cards with chip and tap-to-pay capabilities, the agency noted in the Federal Register on Friday. 

The department contended these payment technologies will help reduce fraud for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that provides food benefits to low-income people.

The proposal comes at a time when the USDA is looking to modernize the SNAP program as well as reduce EBT fraud.

Dive Insight:

The newly proposed rule would require states to issue EBT cards with chip and tap-to-pay technology and also require SNAP-authorized retailers to accept them.

Chip cards are a more secure payment option because cards with chips are harder to copy, making it more difficult to steal SNAP account information, according to the USDA.

The industry trade group National Grocers Association said in a Friday press release that it supports the proposal.

“States that adopted SNAP EBT chip cards have seen a significant drop in skimming fraud, and we appreciate USDA and the [White House] Task Force to Eliminate Fraud for moving every state toward that standard,” Stephanie Johnson, NGA’s senior vice president and head of government affairs, said in a statement.

If the proposal becomes a final rule, states would have two years to comply.

Nearly a dozen states, including California, Oklahoma, Alabama, Michigan, Virginia and Massachusetts, have already issued EBT chip cards to their SNAP participants, and half a dozen more are in the process of doing so, according to the USDA.  

In the proposed rule, the USDA said the transition to chip and tap-to-pay tech for EBT cards “will come at a financial cost to the State agencies administering SNAP and to other entities involved in the operation of EBT systems. However, the Department believes that it is critical for SNAP clients to have reliable and secure access to the benefits that they use.” 

The USDA pointed to the use of these technologies by credit and debit card issuers, noting they have “proven the effectiveness of the technology involved in reducing incidents of fraud.”

Retailers would need to ensure that their point-of-sale machines can accept these types of payment capabilities, the USDA noted. 

The USDA is accepting public comments on the proposed rule until Dec. 22.
